name: Chapel Bridge
label: Chapel Bridge
camera_source: Commons cluster (13 photos). Moved 78 m outwards on 2026-11-10 so it is 110 m from the subject's edge, as the text says.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/396669328: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Kapellbrücke' (201 m across).
notes: Lucerne's iconic covered wooden bridge with its octagonal water tower.

text.description: Chapel Bridge is a covered wooden footbridge that crosses the river Reuss at an angle in the middle of Lucerne, and it is the city's best-known sight. It photographs well because everything comes together in one frame: the long, steep timber roof, the stone water tower standing in the river, and the water below. The bridge was first built around 1365 as part of the town's defences. It is now about 205 metres long, and it is described as the oldest wooden covered bridge in Europe. The octagonal Wasserturm beside it is about 34.5 metres tall and was once used as a prison and a treasury. A fire on 18 August 1993 destroyed much of the bridge and two thirds of its interior paintings. It was rebuilt and reopened on 14 April 1994. Inside the roof are painted panels from the 17th century, showing scenes from Lucerne's history, and some of them have been restored. Switch on the gridlines so the long roofline sits level. Once you have the wide view, walk onto the bridge and photograph the painted panels and the timber beams overhead. Wipe your lens first, as river air and pockets leave smears.
text.geographic_location: In the centre of Lucerne, where the bridge crosses the river Reuss at an angle and links the old town on the right bank with the new town on the left bank. It is named after the nearby St. Peter's Chapel.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so head for the river Reuss in central Lucerne, either from the old town or from the new town on the opposite bank; the bridge joins the two. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the bridge, the tower and some river into one frame, then use the default lens (1x) for a more natural look. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the tower or the roof details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Rathaussteg (smaller footbridge downstream (west) of the Chapel Bridge). A wide shot back along the Reuss toward the covered bridge and the octagonal Water Tower, with the curly railings of the footbridge framing the scene. The bridge lies to the north-east, and from here you can see its long roofline and the tower together.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the bridge's roof with a horizontal line so it does not look tilted. Leave a little water in the foreground, and let the tower sit on one side rather than in the centre. Inside the bridge, use the default lens (1x) and aim along the walkway so the painted panels and beams lead the eye.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the sky or the roof to focus, then slide the exposure down a touch so the sky keeps some colour. Inside the covered part, tap on a painting and lift the exposure slightly. Hold the phone with both hands, as it is darker under the roof.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early in the morning is likely to be quieter on the bridge. In the evening, the softer light is kind to the timber, and night mode can help once it gets dark.

text.access_note: The bridge is a public footbridge, but the water tower is closed to the public, so check the official site before you go.

name: Lion Monument
label: Lion Monument
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Löwendenkmal' (4 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/1485039642: the OpenStreetMap point 'Lion Monument'.
notes: Giant dying lion carved into a sandstone cliff.

text.description:
The Lion Monument (Löwendenkmal) is a huge lion carved straight into a sandstone cliff face, with a quiet pond at its foot. It was designed by Bertel Thorvaldsen and cut in 1820-21 by Lukas Ahorn. It remembers the Swiss Guards killed in Paris in 1792 during the French Revolution. The relief is about ten metres long and six metres high. The lion is wounded by a spear and rests a paw on a shield, with a second shield of the Swiss coat of arms beside it. Mark Twain wrote about the lion mirrored in the pond among the water-lilies, and that reflection is still the picture most people come for.

It works well on a phone because everything sits in one frame: the carved lion, the still water, the ivy-like vines and the trees around it. The best view is from the flat platform on the pond side of the park, straight across from the lion's head. Stepping a little to one side often lets you fit the lion, its reflection and the greenery together without a dead-centre, postcard look. Wait a moment for ripples to settle, as the reflection is much stronger on calm water. If you want a second picture, try the raised part of the park, which gives you the lion from above and to the side with the pond and trees around it. The park has had reconstruction work, so it is worth checking for closures.
text.geographic_location: The monument is in a small park on Denkmalstrasse in Lucerne, set against a rock cliff that was once a sandstone quarry.
text.directions_text: The monument is on Denkmalstrasse in Lucerne. Use a map app to find Denkmalstrasse in Lucerne. Once in the park, head for the pond side, where the phone icon on the map is. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to get the whole lion and its reflection. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are too close to fit the carving and the pond, and keep the lion away from the very edge of the frame. Use telephoto (2x or more) for a close shot of the lion's head and spear.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From here you see the full carved lion in its rock niche with the rectangular pond in front and its reflection in the water. For a different picture, try the raised part of the park, which shows the lion from above and to the side with the pond and trees around it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the water line on the lower third, so the lion fills the top and its reflection fills the bottom. Step a little to one side to fit the lion, the reflection and the greenery into one frame. Hold the phone low and level so the cliff doesn't lean.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the lion's face to focus, then slide the exposure down a touch so the pale stone doesn't wash out. Wait for the water to go still before you shoot.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning or an overcast day, when the light on the lion is even. Going early or at a quieter time of year also means fewer people on the platform.

text.access_note: This is a public park around the monument, but it has had reconstruction work, so check the official site before you go for any closures.

name: Lucerne railway station
label: Lucerne Station
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Schweizerhofquai' (1 web pages); placed at the stretch of Schweizerhofquai nearest the subject (our map tiles); moved 5 m off water.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/2051794005: the OpenStreetMap point 'Luzern'.
notes: Main station with the preserved stone portal of the old building.

text.description:
Lucerne railway station sits right on the lakefront, so the best photos here are of the setting rather than the building itself. The map points you to the lakefront about 300 m north of the station; the lakeside promenade of Schweizerhofquai runs east from the station. From here you can see Lake Lucerne with swans on the water, mountains in the distance and the 19th-century hotel facades along the quay. A guide describes this walk as one of the best photo routes in Switzerland, and on clear days the Alps reflect in the lake.

The station has a long history. The first, wooden station opened on the lake edge in 1856. A larger building with a distinctive cupola followed in 1896. A fire on 5 February 1971 destroyed the frontage and concourse, and the new station opened exactly twenty years later, on 5 February 1991. Santiago Calatrava designed its concourse. In front of the station you can still see the arch of the old building, topped by the sculpture Zeitgeist by Richard Kissling. It makes a good second photo, framed with the lake and mountains behind it, or angled so that the modern glass station front is in the shot.

The square in front is busy with buses and lake boats, so expect people in your frame. Walk a little way along the quay for a calmer view. Check locally that building work is not affecting the square or the arch.
text.geographic_location: In the centre of Lucerne, on the south shore of Lake Lucerne, next to Bahnhofplatz and the boat landing stages.
text.directions_text: Start from the railway station itself, in the city centre. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the lake, the hotel facades and the mountains together. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more of the promenade in the frame. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the swans or to bring the mountains closer.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Schweizerhofquai (lakefront promenade running east from the station). Lake Lucerne with swans and mountains, and the 19th-century hotel facades along the quay; the station is only the starting point of the walk. The railway station lies to the south, behind you, so it is not in this view. Walk back towards the arch in front of the station if you want a photo that includes the station.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the horizon on the upper or lower line. On a clear day, include some of the water so the mountain reflection shows. Use the hotel facades along the quay as a leading line. For the station itself, use the old arch as a frame (Torbogen Luzern) and angle your shot to include the glass front.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the water or the mountains to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky keeps its colour. Keep the phone level, as the gridlines will show if the horizon tilts. Hold still for swans, or use a Live Photo to pick the best frame afterwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a clear day, when the mountains are visible and the lake is calm enough to reflect them. Early morning is usually quieter on the quay.

text.access_note: The quay is an open public street and the arch stands in the public square in front of the station; check the official site before you go for any current building works.

name: Swiss Museum of Transport
label: Swiss Transport Museum
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/135207248: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Swiss Museum of Transport' (366 m across).
notes: Switzerland's most visited museum, with trains, planes and ships.

text.description: The Swiss Museum of Transport (Verkehrshaus der Schweiz) is a large museum beside Lake Lucerne. It covers trains, cars, ships, aircraft, space travel and cable cars. It opened in July 1959 and is described as Switzerland's most popular museum, so it suits a photo stop even if you only have a short time. The grounds are big, with several halls and open-air displays, so there is plenty to frame. Two good outdoor subjects are the submersible Mésoscaphe, built for the 1964 national exhibition, and the paddle steamer Rigi, the world's oldest surviving flush-deck side-wheeler. The outside of the road-transport hall is covered in 344 Swiss road signs. This makes a bold, colourful pattern that works well as a close-up or as a wide shot with a few visitors for scale. Inside, the aviation and space halls hold historic aircraft, a Moon rock and a satellite that came back to Earth. The phone icon on the map sits in the middle of the museum grounds, so you are among the buildings rather than looking at them from a distance. Walk towards the edges of the site for wider views, and take your time with the outdoor vehicles. Photography rules and which areas you can enter may vary, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: In Lucerne, on a large site next to Lake Lucerne. The museum grounds are made up of several halls and open-air displays.
text.directions_text: Start from central Lucerne and head for the lake shore where the museum stands. Once there, the phone icon on the map is in the middle of the museum site. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the big hall fronts and the road-sign facade, and the default lens (1x) for the outdoor ship and submersible. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as individual road signs or the hull of the Rigi.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. For a full-width shot of a hall or the road-sign facade, step back across the open space towards the edge of the site. Photograph the outdoor vessels from a low, side-on position.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the edges of the halls so the verticals stay straight. For the road-sign wall, fill the frame with the pattern, or step back and include a few visitors for scale. With the ships, keep the whole outline in frame and leave a little sky above.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the main subject to focus, then slide the exposure down a touch if the sky is bright so the vehicles and signs keep their colour. Indoors, tap on the exhibit and hold the phone close to any glass to reduce reflections.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Daylight suits the outdoor displays best. A bright but slightly cloudy day gives even light on the signs and vessels.

text.access_note: This is a ticketed museum with outdoor and indoor areas, so check the official site before you go for access and photography rules.

name: Musegg Wall
label: Musegg Wall
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Kapellbrücke' (1 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Kapellbrücke' (way/396669328): middle (201 m across); moved 35 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OSM N413741627 (Musegg Wall): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Medieval city wall with nine towers and city views.

text.description:
The Musegg Wall (Museggmauer) is a stretch of town wall with towers, standing above Lucerne's old town. It works well as a background to an evening photo. Seen from the bridge, the wall sits in the distance, with the Hotel Château Gütsch in the same direction. Around sunset the light glows that way, which gives you warm colour in the sky in the direction of the wall without any need to climb.

Check the exact spot on the map before you set up. From there you are taking a distant view, so think of the wall as one part of a wider evening scene rather than a close-up portrait.

If you want to see the wall closer, there is a second option: the north side, where the wall's towers rise behind the Hotel Château Gütsch. The wall is steep and has a lot of stairs, so allow time and energy for the climb. The towers are open to visitors only in the warmer part of the year, roughly from April to November, so check the official site before you go. The outside views need no access at all.

For a phone photo, keep the horizon level using gridlines, and wait for the sky to colour before you take your main shots.
text.geographic_location: The Musegg Wall stands on the hillside above Lucerne's old town, close to the Hotel Château Gütsch. The Kapellbrücke viewpoint is down by the river, to the south-east of the wall.
text.directions_text: The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to bring the distant wall and towers closer. Use the default lens (1x) for a wider scene with the bridge and sky. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want a close-up of the towers from the wall itself.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Kapellbrücke. The wall in the distance, lit by the sunset light that falls toward the Museggmauer and Château Gütsch. From there the photo shows the Musegg Wall in the distance to the north-west, with the sunset glow in that direction and the Château Gütsch nearby.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the wall on one of the lower lines, leaving most of the frame for the evening sky. Try a 2x or 3x zoom first, then step back to the default lens (1x) for a version that includes the bridge. If you climb up, the north side of the wall shows the towers rising behind the Hotel Château Gütsch.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the wall to set focus, then slide the exposure down slightly so the sunset colours stay rich rather than washed out. As the light fades, try night mode with your phone braced against the bridge rail to keep it steady.

text.access_note: The outside views are from open public space and need no access, but the towers are open to visitors only part of the year, so check the official site before you go.

name: Spreuer Bridge
label: Spreuer Bridge
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Mühlenplatz' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Mühlenplatz' (way/464350689): middle (37 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/396669333: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Spreuerbrücke' (83 m across).
notes: Medieval covered bridge on the Reuss with Dance of Death paintings.

text.description:
The Spreuer Bridge is a covered wooden footbridge across the Reuss in Lucerne, and it is one of only two that survive in the city. The first bridge was built in the 13th century to link Mühlenplatz with the mills in the middle of the river. It was extended to the far bank around 1408, and rebuilt after a flood in 1566. The name comes from the chaff (Spreu) that people were once allowed to dump into the river from this bridge.

Inside the roof, a series of triangular paintings forms a Dance of Death, painted between 1616 and 1637 under Kaspar Meglinger. Of the 67 original panels, 45 survive.

For photos, the best view is from Mühlenplatz, at the mill-side end of the bridge. The red Mühlenturm tower stands in the foreground, and the old town and its walls rise behind. Those layers make the classic postcard shot, and the river gives you a clean strip along the bottom of the frame. If you have time, a second view from the Nadelwehr weir beside the bridge looks back along it, with the river and old town behind.

Take the wide view first, then walk onto the bridge for a few closer shots of the painted panels.
text.geographic_location: The Spreuer Bridge is in Lucerne's old town, crossing the Reuss downriver of the Kapellbrücke. Mühlenplatz, the viewpoint, sits at its mill-side end on the right bank.
text.directions_text: No tram or railway stops are listed for this spot, so head for Lucerne's old town beside the Reuss and look for Mühlenplatz at the mill-side end of the bridge. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to show the bridge, the red tower and the old town together. Try the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you are tight against the buildings and cannot fit the bridge in. Use 2x or more for the painted panels or the tower.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Mühlenplatz (mill-side (right bank) end of the bridge). The covered bridge running across the Reuss, with the red Mühlenturm tower in the foreground and the old town and city walls behind.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines. Put the bridge roof along one of the lower lines and keep a strip of river at the bottom. Let the red tower sit to one side in the foreground, with the old town and walls layered behind. For a different view, the Nadelwehr weir next to the bridge looks back along the span with the river and old town behind.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the bridge to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky does not wash out. Inside the bridge it is dim, so hold the phone steady against a rail or your body, and let night mode work if the app offers it. Live Photos can catch people walking across.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light is kinder to the timber and the red tower than harsh midday sun. Early in the day usually means fewer people on the bridge.

text.access_note: The Spreuer Bridge is a public covered footbridge that you can walk across, but check the official site before you go for any closures.

name: Jesuit Church, Lucerne
label: Jesuit Church
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Kapellbrücke' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Kapellbrücke' (way/396669328): middle (201 m across); moved 35 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/464008694: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Jesuitenkirche' (72 m across).
notes: Early Baroque church beside the Reuss near the old town.

text.description: The Jesuit Church is the first large Baroque church built in Switzerland north of the Alps, and its two green onion-domed towers are easy to pick out along the river Reuss. The river fills the foreground, and the bridge's flower boxes, posts and wooden railings give you a natural frame. Work was begun in 1667, the church was consecrated in 1677, and the onion-topped towers were only finished in 1893. The Jesuits came to Lucerne in 1573 at the city council's invitation to set up a college, and this church grew out of that. For a good photo, keep the two towers centred and the water in the lower third. Use the flower boxes or a post at the edge of the frame, but keep them small so they do not hide the church. If you want a different angle, the Rathaussteg footbridge gives a clear view of the north and east sides of the church, and the Reussbrücke can give a sunrise scene with the Chapel Bridge and the church together. These viewpoints were noted a year or two ago, so check they are still open.
text.geographic_location: The church stands beside the river Reuss in the centre of Lucerne, a short walk from the Chapel Bridge. It sits close to the town hall and the Rathaussteg footbridge.
text.directions_text: Head for the Chapel Bridge (Kapellbrücke) in the centre of Lucerne. You can also take the photo from the bridge without walking to the church at all. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to include the river and the bridge's flower boxes. Then try telephoto (2x or 3x, depending on your phone) to bring the twin towers closer without cutting off the domes. The ultra-wide (0.5x) tends to make the church look small and far away from here, so save it for the church itself or for shots of the bridge.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Kapellbrücke (footpath side of the bridge, shooting back toward the twin towers). The church's two green onion-domed towers across the Reuss, with the river in the foreground and the bridge's flower boxes and posts as framing.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and place the towers on one of the vertical lines, with the water filling the lower part of the picture. Let a flower box, a post or a stretch of wooden railing sit at the edge of the frame as a border. Keep your phone level, as the towers will lean if you tilt it upward. For a different view, the Rathaussteg footbridge shows the north and east sides of the church.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the church to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright, so the green domes keep their colour. Take a Live Photo too: a moving river or passing boat can give you a nicer frame to pick afterwards. If you go inside, photography is only tolerated outside services, so follow any posted signs.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning is a good bet for a calmer bridge and soft light, and a sunrise view with the Chapel Bridge and the church together has been recommended from the Reussbrücke. Dusk also works if you use night mode and brace your elbows on the railing.

text.access_note: The church is an active place of worship, so check the official site before you go for visiting arrangements, and follow posted signs about photography inside; the bridge viewpoint is a public footpath.
claims_not_in_sources: The church is close to the town hall and the Rathaussteg footbridge in the centre of Lucerne.
The bridge is likely to be calmer in the early morning, with softer light.
The ultra-wide lens (0.5x) makes the church look small and far away from the bridge.
Dusk with night mode can work from the bridge.
A moving river or passing boat can make a good Live Photo frame.
Tilting the phone upward makes the towers appear to lean.
The viewpoint is a public footpath on the bridge.

text.description:
The Glacier Garden of Lucerne is an attraction ranked number 8 on the Lucerne map. It suits a phone camera because you will likely find small details close by, so you don't need a big viewpoint to get a good picture. Its ranking makes it a good slower stop between the busier sights.

Walk a little way in before you start. Look for anything with a sense of depth, such as a line leading away from you. Put a person or a bag in the foreground to give a feeling of scale.

Take a few wide shots to show the whole setting, then a few close ones of interesting details. Use anything interesting nearby as foreground. Keep your lens clean, because handling and outdoor air can leave smudges. Take your time, as the best pictures here often come from looking at small things. Check the official site for current opening information before you go.
text.geographic_location: The Glacier Garden is on the Lucerne map. Use the map to see where the Glacier Garden sits among the other spots.
text.directions_text: No tram or railway stop is listed for this spot, so use the map to navigate to the phone icon on the map. Once you reach it, the phone icon on the map is at the site itself, so there is no extra walk to a separate viewpoint. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for most shots. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) for a view that takes in a whole area. Use telephoto/zoom (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for close details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and place a strong line, such as an edge or a path if you find one, along one of the lines to lead the eye into the picture. Keep the phone level, and include something in the foreground for depth. For a close-up, tap the detail to focus and lower the exposure slider slightly so the colours stay rich.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap to focus on the main subject, then drag the exposure slider down a little if bright sky is washing out the scene. Portrait mode can work for a person standing in front of the scene.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Pick a time when the light is soft, such as a bright overcast day or a calm hour outside the middle of the day, which gives gentler shadows and more even detail.

name: Lucerne Culture and Congress Centre
label: KKL Luzern
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Lido' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Lido' (node/4653895622): point.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/1661451: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'KKL Kultur- und Kongresszentrum Luzern' (145 m across).
notes: Jean Nouvel's concert hall with a huge cantilevered roof by the lake.

text.description:
The Lucerne Culture and Congress Centre, usually shortened to KKL, is the big modern concert and congress building on the Lucerne waterfront. French architect Jean Nouvel designed it. It holds a concert hall, an art museum, conference rooms and restaurants. The concert hall opened on 18 August 1998 and the whole complex was inaugurated in March 2000. What you notice first is the huge flat roof, which measures 100 by 100 metres and reaches out over the building like a lid. This is also the main home of the Lucerne Festival.

This spot suits a phone because you shoot the KKL from across the water at the Lido, rather than from right beside it. From there the long, low roof sits above the lake, with the Kapellbrücke and the old town behind it. That gives you a wide lakefront scene with the building as the clear main subject. Because it is a fair distance away, the building will look small at the default lens (1x), so plan to zoom in a little. Keep the horizon level and let the roofline run across the frame. A strip of water in the foreground adds depth. If you also want a different view, the promenade at Schweizerhofquai shows the KKL with the lake, swans and mountains, and the KKL's own terrace looks out over the lake. Check the official site before you go, as the terrace can be closed during events.
text.geographic_location: The KKL stands on the Lucerne lakefront, right beside the lake in the city centre.
text.directions_text: Start from the centre of Lucerne and head east along the lakeshore. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to take in the whole lakefront, then switch to telephoto (2x to 5x, depending on your phone) to bring the KKL and the Kapellbrücke closer. Ultra-wide (0.5x) will make the building very small, so keep it for a close foreground such as railings or plants.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Lido (lakeside Lido area, opposite the KKL across the water). The KKL with the Kapellbrücke and the old town behind it, seen from across the lake.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Put the long roof of the KKL on one of the gridlines and keep the horizon level. Leave a band of lake in the lower part of the frame. Zoom in until the building fills about a third of the width, with the Kapellbrücke still in view. Take one wider shot as well. The promenade at Schweizerhofquai is a good alternative if you want swans and mountains in the picture.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the building to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky keeps its detail. Hold the phone steady with both hands, and take a few frames in a row, because zoomed shots blur easily.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a calm, clear morning or evening, when the light is softer and the lake may be smoother. The roof edge and the water look best then.

text.access_note: The Lido is a public lakeside park area; the KKL terrace and interior may be restricted during events, so check the official site before you go.

name: Rosengart Collection Museum
label: Rosengart Museum
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/1423740030: the OpenStreetMap point 'Rosengart Collection'.
notes: Picasso and Klee collection in a neoclassical former bank.

text.description:
The Rosengart Collection Museum (Museum Sammlung Rosengart) is a modern art museum in Lucerne, built around two artists: Pablo Picasso and Paul Klee. For a phone photographer, the main subject is the building itself. It is a neoclassical former bank, built in 1923-1924 by the Zurich architect Hermann Herter. It once belonged to the Swiss National Bank. The Rosengart family bought it and had it converted by the architect Roger Diener, and it opened as a museum on 26 March 2002. Its calm, formal front makes a tidy, symmetrical photo, with strong straight lines that the gridlines on your phone help you keep level.

Inside, the ground floor shows Picasso, the basement Klee, and the first floor a mix of other artists. The old bank's conference room has been kept as it was and is open to visitors. The Klee holdings are described as the largest in private hands after the artist's family's own. Siegfried Rosengart was an art dealer, and he and his daughter Angela built the collection together.

For your photo, stand at the phone icon on the map and take in the whole façade first. Then move in for smaller shots, such as the entrance, the stonework and any banners or signs. If you plan to go inside, check the official site before you go, both for visiting details and for any rules on photography in the galleries.
text.geographic_location: The museum is in the city of Lucerne, Switzerland, and the subject is the museum building itself.
text.directions_text: No tram or train stops are listed for this spot, so use a map app to find your way from central Lucerne to the museum. Once you arrive, follow the map to the phone icon on the map, which is right at the building. Check the official site before you go for current visiting details. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole façade. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you cannot step back far enough, and to the telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for doorways and architectural details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up the edges of the façade with the vertical lines so the walls do not lean. Take one wide shot of the whole front, then a closer one of the entrance or the stonework. Keep other passers-by out of the frame by waiting for a gap.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the stonework to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright, so the building keeps its detail. If you use the ultra-wide, hold the phone level to avoid stretched edges.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft daylight, such as morning or late afternoon, usually gives the best light on a façade like this.

text.access_note: Check the official site before you go for visiting details and any photography rules inside.

name: Château Gütsch
label: Château Gütsch
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Spreuerbrücke' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Spreuerbrücke' (way/108570986): middle (92 m across); moved 5 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/93508221: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Château Gütsch' (71 m across).
notes: Fairy-tale hotel castle on a hill with views over the city and lake.

text.description:
Château Gütsch is a white, fairy-tale-style castle perched on the Gütsch hill above Lucerne. Today it is a hotel. The building went up in 1888 in a romantic, castle-like style, and in 1901 it was given the look it has now, modelled on Neuschwanstein in Bavaria. Like many grand hotels of its era, it was placed on a high vantage point, here looking over the city and the river Reuss. It reopened in 2014 after a long closure and has 27 rooms.

It photographs best from a distance, where you can see the whole building. The Spreuerbrücke is the recommended place to shoot the château. The pale château rises above the dark forest, with the Old Town rooftops in the foreground. That layering of rooftops, trees and château is what makes the picture work.

From the hotel terrace you get the city, the lake and the Alps, with the château's own façade and entrance in frame. The terrace view is mostly of the city, though, so the château itself is hard to fit in. If you want the panorama, go up to the terrace as a second stop.
text.geographic_location: Château Gütsch stands on the Gütsch hill above Lucerne and the river Reuss.
text.directions_text: From there the château is about 514 m to the west in a straight line, with a climb up the hill. To go up to the hotel, take the Gütsch funicular from Baselstrasse (check that it is running first) or walk up through the Gütschwald forest. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to take in the foreground, the rooftops and the hill together. Then try telephoto (2x or 3x, depending on your phone) to bring the château closer and squeeze the forest and the building together.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Spreuerbrücke. Looking up the Reuss toward the hill, the white château rises above the dark forest, with the Old Town rooftops in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the château on one of the upper intersections, with rooftops filling the lower third. Keep the horizon level. If you also go up to the hotel terrace, use it as a second shot of the city, lake and Alps behind, not for the château itself.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the white façade to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so it keeps its detail against the dark trees. Use 0.5x only if you want a wide shot of the foreground, as it makes the château very small.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning to early afternoon is likely to be kinder, as the sun should then be behind you and fall on the château's front. Late in the day you will be shooting toward the sun, so expect a darker, backlit building.

text.access_note: The château is a private hotel complex, and the funicular and terrace may have their own rules, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: The château lies west of the stand-here point, so in the morning and early afternoon the sun is likely to be behind a photographer there and lighting the château's front.
Late in the day the sun is likely to be in front of the camera when looking at the château from the stand-here point, giving a backlit view.
The walk from the stand-here point to the château involves a climb up the hill; the 514 m figure is a straight-line distance.
The funicular may not always be running, so it is worth checking.

name: Bourbaki Panorama
label: Bourbaki Panorama
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/1485039289: the OpenStreetMap point 'Bourbaki Panorama'.
notes: Giant circular painting of the 1871 Bourbaki army.

text.description:
The Bourbaki Panorama is a huge circular oil painting, 115 metres around, showing a winter scene from February 1871. Thousands of weary French soldiers of General Bourbaki's army cross into neutral Switzerland at the end of the Franco-Prussian War, and local people and Red Cross helpers look after the wounded. Édouard Castres, a Swiss painter who had travelled with the army as a medical volunteer, led the work with a team of ten other artists. It was first shown in Geneva in 1881 and has been in Lucerne since 1889. It was cut down twice, so it is now 9.8 metres tall, about a third less than the original.

It photographs well because you stand in the middle and the scene wraps all the way round you. Real objects, including figures, equipment and a railway carriage, are placed in front of the canvas, so painting and props blend into one scene. This is a rare chance to take a picture that feels like a snowy battlefield-turned-refuge rather than a flat artwork. The painting sits inside a wooden rotunda within a modern glass and steel building.

For your phone, think in two kinds of pictures: wide shots that show the curve and the foreground props, and close details of faces, horses and the meeting of the two generals. Take a few of each, then step back and look for the way rail lines and straight roads lead your eye into the distance.
text.geographic_location: In the city of Lucerne, in a modern glass and steel building that wraps around the old wooden rotunda holding the painting. The building also has shops, a cinema and a restaurant.
text.directions_text: No tram or railway stop is listed for this spot, so start from the centre of Lucerne and go by taxi or hired scooter to the Bourbaki Panorama. Use the phone icon on the map as your destination. Once you are at the building, you are already at the subject. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the sweep of the painting and the props in front of it. Switch to the default lens (1x) for natural-looking views, and the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for faces and small details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Inside, the best position is the centre of the circular painting, where it surrounds you in every direction.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the rail tracks and straight roads, which lead the eye into the distance. Include a little of the real objects in front of the canvas so the picture shows the depth. Then use the telephoto to pick out single groups of soldiers or the meeting of the two generals.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on a bright part of the painting to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the lit areas look washed out. If the room is dim, hold the phone steady against your body or a rail and let night mode take a moment, if your phone offers it. Check the rules on photography before you start taking pictures inside.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Opening times are not given here, so check the official site before you go. Indoor lighting is probably fairly steady, so the time of day may matter less than choosing a quieter moment.

text.access_note: This is likely a ticketed attraction, so check the official site before you go for opening times, tickets and any rules on photography indoors.

name: Richard Wagner Museum, Lucerne
label: Wagner Museum Tribsche
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Richard-Wagner-Weg' (2 web pages); placed at the stretch of Richard-Wagner-Weg nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/87359899: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Richard Wagner Museum' (28 m across).
notes: Villa on the lakeshore where Wagner lived 1866–1872.

text.description:
The Richard Wagner Museum is a cube-shaped manor house on a small mound beside Lake Lucerne, in the Tribschen district. The building dates from the 15th century and took its present form in 1623. The composer lived here from 1866 to 1872 and finished the operas Die Meistersinger von Nürnberg and Siegfried while he was in the house. The city bought the villa and its parkland in 1931, and it opened as a museum in 1933.

It photographs well because the plain, square villa sits in green parkland with the water close by. The easiest picture is the one you get as you walk up the lakeside path, with the house ahead of you and the lake beside you. That gives a simple, balanced shot with a clear sense of arrival. A second, wider view is from the museum park, where the villa can sit in the foreground with the lake and the mountains behind it.

The history gives you extra pictures if you like detail. Wagner's Siegfried Idyll was first played on the villa's stairs on Christmas morning 1870, so the steps and entrance are worth a closer frame. Keep your phone steady and take a few versions, one wide and one a little tighter. If you plan to take photos inside, check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: The museum is in the Tribschen district of Lucerne, on the shore of Lake Lucerne. It stands in its own parkland beside the water.
text.directions_text: No tram or train stop is given for this spot, so start from Lucerne town centre and head to the Tribschen district on the lakeshore. Then follow Richard-Wagner-Weg along the lake to the villa. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the villa seen along the path. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want to include more of the lake and grounds, and keep the house away from the edges of the frame to avoid stretched corners.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Richard-Wagner-Weg (lakeside approach path leading to the museum). The villa seen along the lakeside walk that leads up to it, with the lake beside the path. From here the villa is just ahead of you to the north, with the lake beside the path.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the path up with one of the lower grid lines so it leads the eye to the house. Keep the lake along one side of the frame. For a different view, try the Richard Wagner Museum Park, where the villa sits in the foreground with Lake Lucerne and the mountains behind.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the villa to set focus, then lower the exposure slider a little if the sky or water is bright, so the walls keep their detail. For the closer shot of the steps or entrance, try 2x if your phone has it.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a bright, dry day when the lake and the mountains behind the park are clear. Early or late in the day usually means softer light and fewer people on the path.

text.access_note: The path and grounds appear to be an open walking route, but the museum itself may be ticketed with set opening times, so check the official site before you go.

name: Church of St. Leodegar (Lucerne)
label: Hofkirche St. Leodegar
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Kapellbrücke' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Kapellbrücke' (way/396669328): middle (201 m across); moved 35 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/134989570: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'St. Leodegar im Hof (Hofkirche)' (93 m across).
notes: Twin-towered Renaissance church above the lake.

text.description: The Church of St. Leodegar, known locally as the Hofkirche, is Lucerne's big Catholic church, and its two slim towers are the part you'll recognise from postcards. The best phone photo of it is not taken beside it but from the Kapellbrücke, the covered wooden bridge over the Reuss. From the bridge the timber roof and old beams sit in the foreground, the water runs beneath, and the church towers rise behind. Lucerne's tourism office uses a version of this view, with the towers behind the bridge, to represent the city, and guides point to the same framing. The church was built in parts between 1633 and 1639 after a fire in 1633 destroyed the earlier building. A religious house has stood on this site since the 8th century. In 1874 it also became the parish church, which is why it is still in everyday use. From the bridge the church looks small and far away, so use the bridge as your main subject and let the towers sit above it. If you want a closer picture of the building, walk to its front steps and shoot the facade and twin towers from there. A second option is the Seebrücke, where the church appears along the Nationalquai waterfront with moored boats and lakeside buildings in front of it. Inside, the church is a place of worship, so keep your phone quiet and do not use flash.
text.geographic_location: In the city of Lucerne, near the Reuss, about 618 m north-east of the Kapellbrücke stand-here point.
text.directions_text: Make your way to the Kapellbrücke in central Lucerne. The church lies to the north-east of it, about 10 minutes on foot if you want to go and see it close up. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) so the bridge and the towers both fit in the frame. If the towers look too small, try the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for a tighter picture, but keep some of the bridge in the shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Kapellbrücke. The covered wooden bridge in the foreground over the Reuss, with the two towers of the church rising behind it. The church is to the north-east, so face that way.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and place the church towers on one of the upper lines, with the bridge roof and the river filling the lower part of the picture. Keep the phone level so the towers do not lean. For a different view, the Seebrücke shows the church along the waterfront with boats and lakeside buildings in front, and the front steps of the church give a close picture of the facade and both towers.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the church towers to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky is bright, so the towers keep their detail. Hold the phone steady with both hands, since the bridge can have people walking on it.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft morning or late afternoon light usually suits the towers and the wooden bridge. Early in the day there are usually fewer people on the bridge.

text.access_note: The church is an active place of worship, so dress and behave respectfully inside, avoid flash, and check the official site before you go for opening and service times.

Morning or late-afternoon light usually flatters the towers and the wooden bridge.
There are usually fewer people on the Kapellbrücke early in the day.
The Kapellbrücke can have people walking on it throughout the day.
